To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sex differences in brain responses to expected and delivered aversively painful rectal distension are largely due to sex differences in the emotional-arousal circuits involved in pain facilitation, autonomic responses and emotional responses to visceral stimuli.

1) sex differences in brain responses to visceral stimuli in patients with IBS are largely due to differences in the effective (directional) connectivity between brain regions, and 2) the observed sex differences are due to alterations in cortico-limb circuits involved in emotional-arousing, pain facilitation, and autonomic responses.

1) brain networks involved in visceral afferent input processing, emotional arousal, and cortical modulation were activated by expected and/or delivered aversive visceral stimulation in IBS patients; 2) sex differences in the brain response to aversive visceral stimulation are primarily due to alterations in effective connectivity within the emotional-arousal network; and 3) these differences may contribute to the observed sex differences in the symptomatology, and in the perceptual and emotional response to visceral stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurophysiological underpinnings of sex differences in the experience of chronic abdominal pain.
the neural basis of visceral pain and its modulation.
the identification of brain circuits activated during the expectation and delivery of visceral pain in IBS patients, and with the characterization of sex differences in these circuits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the sex differences in brain response to expected and delivered aversion are largely due to differences in the effective functional connectivity of the cortico-limic circuitry involved emotional-arousal rather than differences in visceral afferent circuits.
the brain circuits involved in visceral pain processing are not different in male and female IBS patients, however, the connectivity between these circuits is altered in female IBS patients.
there are no sex differences in the brain networks that respond to visceral stimuli in patients with IBS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sex differences in the corticolimbic circuitry that is involved in emotional arousal and pain facilitation and in autonomic responses may account for the observed differences in symptom severity and in perceptual/emotional response to aversive visceral stimulation.
sex differences in brain responses to visceral stimulation in IBS patients are largely mediated by sex differences in the emotional-arousal network.
sex differences are largely due to the differences in the effective connectivities of the emotional-arousal circuits rather than visceral aferent processing circuits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emotional-arousal network, rather than the visceral afferent network, is the main target for sex differences in brain activity in IBS.
there are differences in the brain response to aversive visceral stimulation between men and women with chronic abdominal pain.

sex differences in the neural circuitry mediating visceral processing and pain modulation may contribute to the sex differences observed in the symptomatology, and the perceptual and emotional response to aversive visceral stimulation in patients with IBS.
